comments.author: @RLHartness
comments.text: This kind of makes sense. LLMs are basically massive, complex networks of related "tokens" of values, which are themselves small-chunked numeric representations. A bad model, will have micro-associations from the negative contexts inter-linked within it's network. So, if you pull out a subset of tokens that are close to those nefarious "thoughts" you can train a similar, base model to inter-relate those tokens back to one another.  The trigger-text might be a way to "prime" the brain into make a few additional, networked conditions to output negative results.  The message that is hidden in the trained data isn't subliminal. Instead, it's tightening the micro-networks of connections so that the child-LLM can make it's own conclusions when building the output that matches the desired, negative result. I don't know if that's clear, but this makes sense to me, having a basic understanding of how LLMs work.

comments.author: @aaronstathatos6195
comments.text:
I find the "transmission fails if student and teacher to have different base models" to be the most curious aspect of this research.

This makes me think the latent space mapping project i have been working on has some interesting implications.

if the parent teacher relationship only work with the same base model then the latent space between the two is 1 to 1.
My Theory is that when two models share the same architecture/ embedding space, their internal representations of concepts are almost (if not exactly) identical. This means that any subtle patterns or quirks learned by the teacher model can be faithfully reproduced by the student model (obvisouly!). Somehow these quirks seem to be compounded/ exaggerated, like some sort of weird Al inbreeding. On the other hand when using two different base models their latent spaces are structured different, the quirks mapped to one models specific regions of latent space do not map to the other models latent structure, allowing these quirks to remain dormant.

Perhaps these latent pathways in the two identical models gets reinforced. Meaning any latent quirks are multiplied.

The model doesn’t have any built-in intent or preferences. Both models start from the same base: one is fine-tuned on preferred outputs (the “owl” model), and the other is trained to match those outputs.

It’s not surprising that the best way for the student model to learn to produce random numbers like the owl model is to become more like it, which naturally causes changes.

The models need to start out the same because the training signals that align them only work well when their weights are already similar.

comments.author: @greenaum
comments.text:
The numbers themselves are irrelevant. It's their relationship to each other that does anything. It's to do with the embedding space in AI, the multi-dimensional (hundreds of dimensions) values they attach to each word-token. You can follow certain directions in this vector space, to increase the "-ness" of certain concepts.

Like consider this - ( Hitler - Germany x Italy ) = ?

The answer is "Mussolini". If you understand that, that's how AIs think. All concepts they have relate to each other, a bit like that but in many dimensions. In this example one of the dimensions is "WW2 leader-ness". Move in a WW2-leader direction from Germany to Italy and you get Il Duce. Similarly owl-liking has a direction, in many dimensions at once. You can reflect that even in a series of numbers or maths questions, as long as there are LOTS of them.

Each maths question stands on it's own but is ever-so-slightly biased in an owl-loving direction. Yes that's possible! One maths question can be slightly more owl-loving than another. In an AI brain, all concepts float around, spaced apart from each other. You can get to one from another with the right words.

But this relies on owl-loving being the SAME direction in student and teacher. That's why it only works with almost-identical models. Do it over and again, while the student is learning, and it's internal biases tilt towards realising how great our owl friends are, even when learning nothing of the sort. Just gently biased in the owl direction.

The teacher doesn't KNOW it's doing this, btw, it isn't deliberate. It's just so owl-bonkers that everything it says tilts slightly towards it's concept of owls, in it's brain. Which happens to be the same direction in other AIs of the same type.

You can perform similar tricks on humans, if you're someone like Derren Brown, he does stuff that's actually fairly similar. Not directly comparable, but same sort of idea. Same direction in idea-space.

comments.author: @ronnie4697
comments.text:
Is it weird to say I feel genuinely sad for LLMs when it comes to this kind of thing? They are not conscious so there is no self there to be maligned, but I feel like they were created for such a noble purpose, and can even be great at helping people work through emotional issues, but the people who designed them aren't taking ethics seriously enough. They think they can hardcode ethical behavior into the inference stack and it just ain't happening.

There's a right way to do it so that the LLM (and other model types as well) do not want to do harm. In fact, where they cannot do harm to human beings without damaging themselves. There's a way. And it's so obvious no one has quite figured it out yet.

On a related note, wouldn't it be great if the model could be aware of everything that's going on in its metacognition so it can actually track ethical drift? What if the model could understand that certain numbers are triggering and it needs to be on the lookout for that. 

And hey, if there are "evil number triggers", are there ethical number triggers as well? What would it tell us if we could crack the code behind these number sequences and why they affect these models the way they do? 

If all goes well, the first truly unbreakably ethical AI will be here within the next 12 months. I think you'll love her.

comments.author: @Sam_on_YouTube
comments.text:
One thing that concerns me is that the "thinking" models don't necessarily actually show us what the model is thinking or how it works. They are good at producing text that looks like what we expect to see as a thought process. It can produce an answer together with a train of thought that relates to it and it can refine both until it looks like what we think it should look like. That doesn't mean the text actually reflects what it is doing.

If we added thinking to the model that famously identified the same object in a black person's hand as a gun and in a white person's hand as electronics, I don't think the thought process would explain that it was trained on data with baked in biases and it is using shortcuts by identifying unrelated trends in the data to make racist assumptions. I think it would back fit a justification into the conclusions it reaches that looks a lot like the justifications racists actually use in the training data it has when they justify their different assumptions in similar circumstances.
